title: 上线第一周就会撞上的 5 种语音智能体失败模式 — Venky B，Plivo
author: AI Engineer
content:
Brief Description

Venky B, founder and CEO of Plivo (calling himself chief agent officer), walks through five production failure modes that hit voice AI agents in week one: latency tradeoffs across the speech pipeline, brittle speech-to-text under real-world noise and code-switching, structured data collection treated as typed fields rather than free transcript, TTS normalization between the LLM and synthesis, and turn detection plus barge-in and backchanneling. Drawing on Plivo’s full-stack voice platform and over a billion voice calls a month, he shows what works in production—open-source LLMs for sub-300 ms targets, dynamic keyword boosting and LLM post-processing for transcripts, field-level schemas and unit-test evals for collection accuracy, and an in-house normalization layer so agents stay portable across TTS vendors.

Table of Contents

  • From Proof of Concept to Production
  • Plivo’s Journey and Full-Stack Voice Platform
  • The Default Voice Agent Pipeline
  • Failure Mode 1: Latency, Cost, and Intelligence
  • Failure Mode 2: Brittle Transcriptions
  • Failure Mode 3: Collecting Structured Data
  • Failure Mode 4: TTS Normalization
  • Failure Mode 5: Turn Detection, Barge-In, and Backchanneling
  • Closing

From Proof of Concept to Production

Let’s do a couple of quick questions and then jump right in. How many of us in the room have built voice AI agents? That’s a pretty good audience. And how many of you have built AI agents that have been deployed in production? Not bad.

Everyone’s talking about voice AI agents—the one-pill solution to pretty much everything in the world today. Everyone’s building one and trying to deploy it. They sound great when you’re building in your dev landscape, and then the moment you take them from proof of concept to production, things start failing. We’ll walk through five different angles of what we’ve seen at Plivo with voice AI agents.

Plivo’s Journey and Full-Stack Voice Platform

A quick intro from my side: I am Venky, the founder and CEO. She used the title agent engineering manager; I’m calling myself chief agent officer from a title standpoint.

Why are we even qualified for this discussion, and what are we seeing that a lot of companies don’t get to see? We’ve been around for about 14 years. Our journey has been a developer API platform and now an AI agent business. We started with voice and SMS APIs back in 2011, and now we are primarily focused on our AI agent offering—the full stack on our platform. We see over a billion voice calls each month across the globe, which is where we’ve seen a lot of these patterns emerge when we work with customers on their voice agents in production. We’re a 90-member team and have 50 million in funding in the bank. Fun fact: this is not from external VC investors. This is all from being a profitable company and putting that cash in the bank over these years.

Some customers we power across the globe—we’ve left some logos in there. From an offering standpoint, I would cohort this into three buckets. One is a programmable AI agent offering. It’s a speech pipeline, not a true speech-to-speech product yet, but it’s a programmable offering. We also have an AI agent studio, a no-code visual builder. And like I said, we started with voice APIs, so we’ve built out SIP trunking and audio streaming layers over the last 14 years. We don’t rely on other folks for the telephony or carrier layer—that’s the bread-and-butter business we’ve built over all these years, and that’s on top of which our AI agent platform sits.

The Default Voice Agent Pipeline

With that, let’s get into this. Since you guys have all built AI agents, you’ve all seen this or built it in one manner or another. We’ll spend more time on how the entire pipeline looks.

What we see with customers—and I’m sure you can all relate—is that anyone thinking about AI agents picks a bunch of orchestration frameworks and does a pretty good job: LiveKit or Pipecat, build their AI agent on top of that. They think they can just orchestrate these different four layers—speech-to-text, LLM, and TTS, with turn detection in between—and they’re off to the races. My AI agent works in a PoC and it’s good to go in production. Typically that’s what happens. They measure their latencies—you can see some indicative latencies on this slide at each layer—and they’re like, yeah, this seems good for what I need. So they position for production, and then the production woes start to kick in, and you see all sorts of failure modes, which we’re going to spend most of this talk on. I’ve kept some time at the end for Q&A if you want questions, but we’ll jump right into the different failure modes we see.

Failure Mode 1: Latency, Cost, and Intelligence

Let’s start with the first one, which everyone talks about—the most spoken-about failure mode, which is latency. I think we have a few AI agent talks today. I’m pretty sure everyone is going to touch upon this specific failure mode, which is why I’m bringing it right up in terms of how this entire experience is for users.

Typically most folks measure this by time to first audio: the time from when the user stops speaking to when your agent starts speaking. If you’ve built voice agents, you’ve probably seen what good or natural feels like, what noticeable feels like, and what annoying feels like—different tiered steps. We notice most people want to be under 550 milliseconds, because that’s what’s advertised by platforms or solutions or layers. But I think most end up between 750 milliseconds to 1.2 seconds. That’s where most folks end up. The really bad-performing ones end up at more than 1.2 seconds, and then you start to see users hang up.

I’ll share what we’ve seen practically in production with customers at different layers, and then solutions to some of these. The way we want to think about this layer is as a balance between three things: cost, intelligence, and latency. Why do I bring these three up? Because they’re interrelated.

One of the things over the last year is that we’ve seen a lot of innovation and a lot of intelligence spike on the LLM side. Most of that intelligence has come in terms of thinking or reinforcement learning and so on. The irony with voice agents is that almost always the LLM or the agent that’s talking has to have thinking turned off. So all the advancements we’ve had in the LLM layer in the last year—none of that even applies here now. You obviously have better models that can do better instruction following or tool calling, but pretty much all of your intelligence that’s been built on the thinking layer is off by default if you want it to be fast enough. That’s one of the ironies we come up with. So then how do you balance intelligence, cost, and latency?

Let’s look at some of the options out there in the market. I’m specifically picking LLM because if you looked at the previous chart, LLM is sort of your highest latency bucket that adds to this. If you look at frontier models—which I think most folks start with by default, your OpenAI, your Claude, your Geminis—P50 time to first token is roughly around 450 to 500 milliseconds on a good day, and it can get spiky. P90 and P95 can go easily upwards of 1.2 to 1.3 seconds, and that’s not good for the overall agent experience.

That’s your frontier model. Now there’s another option, which is your Cerebras or Groq, famous and popular for spitting out a lot of tokens very fast. These work, but for you to get dedicated latency or time to first token on these, you need dedicated capacity, and that is really expensive—that’s where I spoke about cost as one of the things to balance. It’s really expensive. If you talk to anyone from the Groq team or the Cerebras team, they’ll tell you you need to book 12 months in advance for dedicated capacity; they’re booked out for the next 12 months. So that’s a pretty expensive option, and you really need to be sure that the model you’re deploying on some of these infra layers will be here 12 months from now. It’s a big investment and a big unknown.

So what’s a realistic option for production-grade agents that are good quality and end up balancing these three? This is what has worked for us: open-source models. There are obviously a lot of them in terms of variety and variations you can pick. I’m specifically talking about the two we work with: Qwen 3.5 and Gemma 4. These are kind of cutting-edge open-source models out in the market right now, and we’ve done a lot of benchmarking around how they work.

It can be scary to think, okay, I have the models now, I have to host them, run them on my own GPUs, and so on. But if you are consistently targeting under 300 milliseconds, we’ve seen this to be a great option to balance latency, cost, and intelligence.

Some more deep dive here: if you’re doing only English, Qwen 3.5 or Gemma both work fine. But if you’re doing multilingual—international audiences, different languages—Gemma 4 is a much better model for that. We’ve seen token fertility evals. Essentially, if I were to dejargonize that, it means how many tokens does it take to generate one word in that language. Gemma is much better—at least 2.5 to 3x better than Qwen 3.5 from that perspective—so your time to words is much faster on Gemma, everything else equal, on a multilingual basis.

What sizes do you pick at the LLM layer? The mixture-of-experts usually works fine. The three- or four-billion mixture-of-experts usually works fine. The problem with mixture-of-experts is that if anyone wants to go down the direction of fine-tuning, that can be a challenge, because fine-tuning mixture-of-experts models is not easy. You can end up breaking the model a lot of times. So that’s one challenge we see with mixture-of-experts. But usually out of the box it gets you 90% closer to where you want to be, even without any fine-tuning or custom work done on the model. That’s the advantage of mixture-of-experts.

Now, if you want to fine-tune and go deeper and say, look, I’m working for a specific domain—healthcare, what have you—and I want to make sure I’m able to fine-tune my model, you want to start at least with the 8-billion or 12-billion from where we are today. Maybe six months from now a 4-billion model beats the 8-billion model hands down. But for today, what we’ve seen is you minimum need an 8-billion or 12-billion model, because you’re looking for two things in these models: one, obviously fast tokens but good instruction following; and second, a very high success ratio in tool calling. If you can do these two things well, then you are 70–80% there from not even having to fine-tune any model—models will work out of the box.

That’s been our recipe. We actually run two flavors: one, a fine-tuned model for specific industries, and then for most generic use cases, an MoE model just works out of the box. There are a few more tips and tricks we’ll talk about in the upcoming slides where we see failure modes, but that’s where we stand from a latency and LLM standpoint.

I’m running tight on time, so I’m going to fast-track this. There are a couple of other flavors. People build agents with a mixture of models. What they do is, for the talking part of it, they have a conversational model which is a much smaller model—maybe even a three-billion model—and then for tool calling they have a much larger model so that they have an improved tool-calling success ratio there.

Failure Mode 2: Brittle Transcriptions

The second one is: assume your transcriptions are going to be brittle. That’s something you want to live by when you’re building AI agents, even if you have the best transcription engine out there. I’ll show you why.

The state-of-the-art transcription engines out in the market sort of get you to a 4% to 6% word error rate. This is on known eval sets. On real-world noisy calls with people having different accents, domain vocabulary, and so on, those usually end up in the double digits from a word error rate perspective. You can obviously fine-tune—pick up an open-source model and fine-tune—but we see typically what breaks here often, and there are patterns in terms of what breaks: proper nouns, jargons, phone numbers—random missing digits with phone numbers—wrong substitutions. I’ll walk through some examples of how you solve for these. Addresses: when you’re trying to collect a long address, the transcription engine could just end up missing some parts of it.

Code-switched languages—I’ll take an example of a language I speak because that was easy for me to put on the slide—where if you were to take English but written in a different script, that’s what’s used for Hindi. This is English written in that script, whereas the actual English version of this is “hello how are you.” So if I’m addressing an audience in a different country where I have code-switched languages and I start getting my English in a different script, everything starts breaking from the transcription engine to the LLM layer and then beyond, because your LLM starts then producing output in that sort of script a lot of times, and then your TTS messes up. This is very important to be careful about. If you want to build your agent independent of the transcription engine, you need to build a layer that normalizes all of this. We’ll talk about solutions in a minute.

And there is the other case, which is Hindi in Latin or Roman—Hindi that reads English—which again messes up everything downstream. Those are just examples. This applies to Arabic, Mandarin, Japanese, what have you—pretty much any language.

So what actually moves the needle at the transcription layer? For proper nouns, we recommend not just keyword boosting. A lot of transcription engines provide keyword boosting where you can put specific words into their engine, but doing dynamic keyword boosting. What that means is: don’t keep the keyword for the entire state of the call; just add that dynamically when you think you need that as an answer so that you get the highest accuracy. Meaning at different states of the call, the transcription engine will have different keywords boosted during different phases. That’s what we’ve seen works best, because if you just pollute your context of the transcription engine with tons of keywords, it’ll start hallucinating again. So that’s what we see typically working best.

Post-process your transcripts with an LLM, because your LLM has domain context and your transcription engine does not. So a lot of words that it would say—I’ll give you some examples—may not make sense. This is a transcription like a phone number from a transcription engine. What do you think that E is? If you give it to an LLM, it knows that’s a three. Similarly, what that “one” is—it’s a digit one. So your transcription engine a lot of times could mess that up, but when you post-process it with the LLM layer, it’ll instantly correct that from a collection standpoint.

And the last one, like I said: transliteration. Your STT output that’s multilingual also gets normalized using either an LLM you first transliterate with, or some kind of neural transliteration engine. There are a lot of them open source; you can just pick one of them. That would do all of that work for you—send cleaned transcripts consistently, independent of the transcription engine, to your LLM.

Failure Mode 3: Collecting Structured Data

The third one we typically see is collecting data. This is where I think 50% to 60% of AI agents mess up pretty badly. We like to think of it as a UX problem, but just for voice. So think data models—and not a transcript coming into an LLM and trying to figure out what the transcript said.

Let’s take some inspiration from—I’m assuming most of us are developers here—Python’s data classes, Pydantic, Zod from TypeScript, or form fields in the UI. If you start thinking of it from that problem statement, we have seen accuracy grow from 30% to like 95% from a data collection standpoint when you start thinking in that manner.

Decide your shape before you ask. Instead of keeping it open-ended, can you keep it constrained? Can a phone number be a phone-number-type field? The moment you do that, you know how many digits it needs to have. You can do validation on top of that, and what sort of allowed values can even be there. So in the previous example we saw, if an E comes in in the middle of a phone number and you know it’s a phone number, you instantly know either you smart-guess that to three and confirm that with a user, or you know that’s an error and then you’ve validated that and asked the user to repeat again. That’s one of the common patterns we’ve seen here from a collection pattern.

Name I think is the interesting one. I’ve just picked a hard-to-pronounce name. There’s no way a human is going to get this right, and no way a transcription engine will get this right, however many times you do this. So the moment you start thinking of this as fields and then have rules and confirmation mechanisms on spelling this letter by letter, only then you kind of get it right. Otherwise it’s going to mess up pretty badly in terms of how you collect this on a voice call. That’s just an example of what I’m talking about in terms of the data collection piece of it.

Another place where it goes badly dramatically is relative values. Date being one of the examples. If somebody says “next week Wednesday 8,” 8 could mean 8:00 a.m. or 8:00 p.m., and then figuring out what that date actually is again becomes a very constrained problem if you knew this was a datetime field and I’m collecting a datetime field, and then you take the current date and figure out what this value would be based on that. That’s how you want to make sure you do this with a combination of the LLM with the tool calling, and the tool calling is doing a lot of this heavy lifting for you from a field standpoint.

And then you run this from a unit-test perspective. So all of your evals need to start treating these fields as unit tests. As long as your unit tests validate and pass, you know your agent is going to be reliable and repeatable. You don’t run hundreds of end-to-end agent test cases just to find out one field collection is broken. You do your eval at a field level and a unit-test level.

Like I said, this mindset makes everything more structured instead of hoping I’ll put a ton of prompt, keep changing the prompt by a few characters every time, and somehow my prompt engineering is going to make the LLM much more instruction-tuned and magically start following some of these things. In fact, like I said, we have seen us get to 95–97% accuracy without having to fine-tune a model. And the trick is basically just breaking down your context of what the agent is doing at that point with specific states of what the agent is going through.

Failure Mode 4: TTS Normalization

I’m just going to quickly skip through this from a time standpoint. I just see I got three more minutes—hopefully that’s a bug, but we’ll leave it at that.

So this is the fourth area where we see issues coming in. Most folks take the LLM output and then send it to a TTS. Obviously there are a lot of good TTSes in the market that take care of a lot of heavy lifting, but a lot of times it messes up. What we recommend and what we’ve seen is you usually want to have a normalization layer between your LLM and what is fed to a TTS. You don’t send your LLM output directly to a TTS. We’ll just walk through some examples.

The basics: strip emojis and markdown before any synthesis into the TTS. Most orchestration pipelines do this—a LiveKit or a Pipecat would do that for you if you just set a few flags. But just make sure if you’re not using them or building from scratch that you’ve set this explicitly, because you don’t want an emoji showing up on something read out, or markdown showing up there.

Some more common ones: custom dictionaries. Most TTS engines provide this to you—how to pronounce custom words, whether it’s proper nouns, brands, acronyms, and so on. So set those in when you go from your LLM to your TTS output, because if you don’t, you’re going to mess that up. I’ll show you an example of how we test that.

The other one is that most engines also give you speed. So if you know you’re pronouncing an entity, slow down. Have your agent slow down—to 0.8x or 0.7x—so that it’s able to enunciate on that specific entity and doesn’t mess up how it’s pronouncing an email or a phone number or a name letter by letter.

And yeah, just normalize all the messy stuff: emails, currency, dates. Don’t leave it to the TTS to do it. Most of them do it, but don’t leave it to the TTS to do it. Build your normalization layer at your end so that tomorrow if you think you need to switch TTS, or for whatever reason the first one’s down and you want to use another TTS, you’re able to not rely natively on the TTS’s engine—you are building this in-house for this to be managed.

I don’t have my badge here, but I don’t have my last name on that, so my first test is: if it cannot pronounce my last name or my company’s name, it’s already dropping the ball. My last name is Balasubramanian, and if you cannot pronounce that using a voice AI agent, that’s a check for me. I know the agent will mess up a lot of words that need to be spelled out day by day. The second one is our company name, Plivo. A lot of engines pronounce it “pivo” or “pleo” and so on. But specifically being able to control this in your pipeline is super critical. And then if you’re building a customer-facing product, give this option to your customers.

Failure Mode 5: Turn Detection, Barge-In, and Backchanneling

I’m just going to skim through the last two slides. I’m running badly over time.

Turn detection—I think this is its own separate topic, but I’m just going to quickly pull up all the points so you guys can skim through that, and if you need a chat after this we can talk about this. I’m just going to leave that for like five seconds and then we can chat about this offline. I’m quite over time.

And then the last one is barge-in and backchanneling. I think there’s a lot of talk around speech-to-speech models that do some of this, but we’ve been able to see how we could do all of this in speech-to-text pipelines. You really don’t need a speech-to-speech model to do all of this. Again, I’ll just put this up on the slide and sort of close at that.

Closing

All right, I don’t think we have time for questions. We can take them offline if you have any time. But hopefully this was helpful and gave you some insights on what we are seeing in production with billions of calls at scale. All right, thanks.
aiSummary: Plivo 创始人 Venky B 梳理语音 AI 智能体上线第一周常见的五种生产失败模式：延迟与成本、智能的权衡，脆弱的 STT，结构化数据采集，TTS 归一化，以及轮次切换，并分享来自月通话量超十亿平台的落地配方。
oneSentenceSummary: Plivo 创始人 Venky B 梳理语音 AI 智能体上线第一周常见的五种生产失败模式：延迟与成本、智能的权衡，脆弱的 STT，结构化数据采集，TTS 归一化，以及轮次切换，并分享来自月通话量超十亿平台的落地配方。
summary: Venky B，Plivo 创始人兼 CEO，指出语音 AI 智能体在 PoC 阶段往往表现稳健，一上生产却容易崩盘。他以 Plivo 的全栈语音管线（非 speech-to-speech）以及每月超十亿次语音通话为背景，逐一拆解团队在第一周常撞上的五种失败模式。谈延迟时，他把成本、智能与速度看成三角形：前沿模型的 P50 首 token 时延约 450–500 ms（P90/P95 常超过 1.2 s），专用的 Groq/Cerebras 容量又贵又难约；开源模型如 Qwen 3.5、Gemma 4 可瞄准 300 ms 以内，通用路径用 MoE，需要微调与工具调用可靠性时则用 8B–12B 稠密模型。他把 STT 视为野外脆弱环节（WER 常达两位数），建议按通话状态做动态关键词增强、LLM 后处理与音译归一化。把电话号码、姓名、日期时间等当作带类型校验的结构化字段（类似 Pydantic/Zod），再配合字段级单元测试评测，据说可将采集准确率从约 30% 拉到 95–97%。在 LLM 与 TTS 之间自建归一化层（去掉 markdown/emoji、发音词典、对实体放慢语速）可让智能体跨厂商可移植。轮次检测、打断与附和因时间不够只草草带过，并主张 speech-to-text 管线无需 speech-to-speech 模型也能覆盖这些能力。

mainPoints.point: 延迟是成本–智能–速度的三角形，不是单一 SLA 追逐
mainPoints.explanation: 前沿模型 TTFT 的 P50 常落在 450–500 ms，尾部会冲过 1.2 s；专用高速算力既贵又常约满。Plivo 的生产配方偏向瞄准 300 ms 以内的开源模型：通用路径用 MoE，微调与工具调用占主导时则用更大的稠密模型。

mainPoints.point: 默认 STT 很脆弱，先归一化再让 LLM 采信
mainPoints.explanation: 干净评测上 4–6% 的 WER，到嘈杂、口音重、领域术语多的真实通话常变成两位数。按通话状态做动态关键词增强、用 LLM 做转写后处理，再加音译归一化，才能避免专有名词、数字、语码切换与文字系统错误一路级联到 LLM 与 TTS。

mainPoints.point: 采集结构化字段，别指望自由文本转写碰运气
mainPoints.explanation: 把电话号码、姓名、日期时间当作带校验与确认的类型化字段，并用字段级单元测试代替只跑端到端评测——讲者称这一思路把采集准确率从约 30% 推到 95–97%，且无需模型微调。

mainPoints.point: 自建 TTS 归一化层，才能随时换厂商
mainPoints.explanation: 去掉 emoji 与 markdown，应用发音词典，对难读实体放慢语速，并在自有层里归一化邮箱、货币与日期，而不是把发音交给各家 TTS。这样才能稳住发音控制，并在厂商故障或品牌名读错时快速切换。

mainPoints.point: 轮次切换仍然关键，但本场只草草带过
mainPoints.explanation: 轮次检测、打断与附和被标为生产关键能力，并声称 STT 管线无需 speech-to-speech 模型也能做到；但因讲者超时，这一节几乎只剩幻灯片略过。

keyQuotes: 在开发环境里听起来很棒，一旦从概念验证推到生产，事情就开始崩。
语音智能体的讽刺之处在于：几乎总是，正在说话的那个 LLM 或智能体必须关掉 thinking。
第二条是：默认你的转写会很脆弱。
如果你从那个问题定义出发去想，我们看到数据采集准确率可以从 30% 做到大概 95%。
不要把 LLM 的输出直接送给 TTS。
